title: Vermont Has Spent Nearly a Billion Dollars to Clean Up Lake Champlain. But the Green Slime Keeps Coming Back.
author: John Dillon
content:
On the last day of August, Jeff van den Noort spotted thick swirls of neon
green film coating the water just steps from his home in Vermont. He waded in
up to his ankles and dipped a jar to get a sample of the scum.

It wasn’t the first time he’d seen the slime. Since his parents bought the
house on an island in Lake Champlain in 1966, van den Noort has spent part of
nearly every summer in this quiet spot. Back then, the lake was clear.

But he began to witness the water’s deterioration as he grew older, especially
after he moved into the home full time in 2010 to care for his ailing mother.
That day in late August was the worst he’d seen all summer.

Later that week, van den Noort grabbed a bucket, a few Mason jars and a
smartphone and got into his rusty Saab. He drove past the boat launches,
frozen-in-time general stores and windswept pastures of the lake’s islands in
northern Vermont and stopped at four other spots along the shore. Each time,
he collected some murky water, gauged how thick the muck was, took a few
photos and jotted down the weather conditions. He then uploaded his report to
an online database.

Van den Noort was one part of a large volunteer effort to monitor a problem
that has plagued Lake Champlain, which supplies drinking water to about
200,000 people. In recent decades, blooms of potentially toxic cyanobacteria,
often called blue-green algae, have killed pets, forced beaches to close and
hurt business and property values along the shores of this iconic Vermont
feature.  

“I just don’t feel like enough is being done,” van den Noort said. “And I
think the state needs to take this seriously.”

![A close-up view of thick, pea green water coating plant
material.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/Marshland_Shore_Close-
crop_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)A
cyanobacteria bloom mixes with duckweed on the shoreline of Lake Champlain in
the town of St. Albans, Vermont, in early August. Courtesy of Lake Champlain
Committee

Just over a decade ago, state leaders seemed to be doing just that. In 2015,
then-Gov. Peter Shumlin stood a few feet from Lake Champlain by the Burlington
waterfront and signed Vermont’s Clean Water Act. It promised to tighten limits
on pollution and provide funding to clean up the state’s waterways.

The move was a response to ratcheting pressure from environmentalists and the
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA had been telling Vermont
officials for years that they needed to take much stronger action. In 2016,
the agency finalized tougher cleanup targets that the state must meet by 2036.

But after 10 years and nearly a billion dollars spent on water quality
projects and programs, Vermont’s cleanup effort is faltering. In a little-
noticed letter to the head of Vermont’s Department of Environmental
Conservation last year, the EPA’s regional administrator warned that the state
was “not on track” to meet its cleanup goal and would need to more than double
its annual pace.

Halfway through the two-decade timetable, Vermont has achieved only 35% of the
goal, according to the state’s most recent estimates. And the steps that
Vermont has taken to get there, such as upgrading sewage treatment plants,
represent “low-hanging fruit,” Eric Perkins, a former EPA official involved in
setting the target, wrote in an email in response to questions from Seven Days
and ProPublica.

The culprit behind these blooms is phosphorus, an element that is an essential
building block of life, present in all organic matter. But too much of it has
been pouring into the lake from farm fields saturated with fertilizer and
manure, dirty stormwater, and raw sewage from treatment plants overwhelmed by
heavy rains. That has tipped the lake’s ecosystem out of balance, spurring the
growth of microorganisms that turn shallow bays and shorelines into no-go
zones.

Ingesting cyanobacteria-laden water can cause vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness
and liver damage, while skin contact can lead to rashes. Researchers have also
detected possible links between chronic exposure to cyanobacteria and
heightened risk of Parkinson’s disease and ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig’s
disease. The algae blooms can also deprive fish and other aquatic life of
oxygen.

While some areas of Lake Champlain have seen incremental improvements in
phosphorus concentrations and cyanobacteria blooms, other parts of the lake
are getting worse. Seven of the lake’s 15 sampling stations have exceeded the
EPA’s annual phosphorus limits every year since 2015, a Seven Days and
ProPublica analysis of lake monitoring data through 2025 shows. Four stations
recorded higher average phosphorus levels over the past decade than in the
decade before, including in the southern part of the lake and its northeast
arm.

![Groups of people wearing swimsuits lie on the beach and play in a lake.
Hills covered in vegetation and buildings can be seen on the other
shore.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20260907-Kenna-
VT-
Champlain-38_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=2560)People
enjoy the water at North Beach on Lake Champlain in Burlington, Vermont, on
Labor Day weekend. Algae blooms sometimes force the city to close the beach.
Caleb Kenna for ProPublica

In September, the Department of Environmental Conservation reported to the EPA
that in two northeastern sections of the lake most chronically plagued by
phosphorus runoff, the state is not nearly on track to meet its targets. The
department specifically acknowledged that it was not making enough progress in
addressing stormwater runoff and that reductions in farm pollution in the
Missisquoi River watershed have slowed since 2023.

Vermont shares the 120-mile-long lake with New York and Quebec, but it’s the
source of about two-thirds of the phosphorus that flows into the water body.
Agriculture is the largest polluting sector, while stormwater runoff from
development, like urban parking lots and rural roads, contributes the highest
amount of phosphorus per acre.

State agencies have repeatedly delayed taking more difficult and politically
fraught action to crack down on pollution from farms, businesses and housing
developments. Policies around them have encountered resistance from the dairy
industry, property owners and lawmakers sympathetic to their interests.

The challenges in cleaning up Lake Champlain raise a salient question: If a
small, conservation-minded state like Vermont can’t tackle this problem, what
does that mean for other areas of the United States grappling with algae
blooms in the Great Lakes, the Chesapeake Bay and the Gulf of Mexico?

State officials counsel patience as they remind Vermonters it will take more
time to solve the problem.

“We are moving apace with the commitments we’ve made, in terms of the
projects, but it isn't manifesting itself nearly as quickly in the lake
monitoring data,” said Julie Moore, Agency of Natural Resources secretary.
“This is a complex ecosystem, and we need to come at this work with a whole
lot of humility.”

Leaders of the Agency of Agriculture, Food and Markets said it will take time
for investments, such as programs to reduce soil erosion and help farmers
upgrade their manure storage equipment, to pay off.

“The first five years, we were really developing an enormous amount of
programs,” said Laura DiPietro, the agency’s water quality program director,
but implementing them “doesn’t happen overnight.” She said she expects to see
greater phosphorus reductions resulting from them in the coming decade.

But for van den Noort, the blooms are increasingly hard to ignore.

“The worst days ever are really, really bad,” he said. “Just as far as you can
see, the whole bay is green.”

![A close-up view of green, turquoise and white sludge-like water with
bubbles.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_9521-2x3-crop_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)In
September, van den Noort found turquoise and white patches of cyanobacteria in
the lake. Scientists say the blooms turn those colors when they break down,
potentially releasing toxins in the water. Jeff van den Noort ![An aerial view
of a piece of land jutting into gray water. Trees with yellow, orange and
green foliage cover the land, and a building with a gray roof can be
seen.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261007-Kenna-
VT-
Champlain-5-2_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)One
of van den Noort’s routine cyanobacteria monitoring sites in North Hero,
Vermont. Caleb Kenna for ProPublica

### Pushing the Limits

Unlike chemicals and heavy metals that can be removed from lakes and rivers
with dredging, phosphorus isn’t technically or economically feasible to
extract.

So environmental regulators focus instead on limiting the amount of phosphorus
that flows into the water each day. It’s like putting the lake on a diet. The
EPA sets what’s known as the total maximum daily load, a target based on the
agency’s determination of how much phosphorus the lake can absorb and remain
healthy. To meet that goal, the state must cut pollution from agriculture,
stormwater drains, roads, forests and wastewater treatment plants.  

The EPA had set previous targets for Lake Champlain in 2002, but, concerned
that Vermont wasn’t taking strong enough measures, the agency set tougher ones
in 2016. For the first few years after those targets were updated, Perkins,
who was then the EPA’s Vermont water quality coordinator, felt that the state
was generally on the right track.

During his tenure, state agencies and lawmakers set up the Clean Water Fund to
finance water quality projects and dedicated tax revenue streams to support
it. They put in place stronger rules for fertilizer use and manure storage on
farms. They created permit programs to limit stormwater runoff from roads and
municipalities. That progress was reflected in a 2020 report card the EPA
issued, acknowledging that Vermont had checked off all the milestones up to
that point.

“Overall, I was very impressed with the level of commitment demonstrated by
the state,” Perkins wrote to Seven Days and ProPublica.

By the time Perkins retired in 2021, he and colleagues at the EPA had become
concerned about signs of lagging commitment by Vermont’s agencies to water
quality enforcement on farms.

![Silhouettes of a couple of people who are swimming in a lake as boats float
by under a cloudy sky.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20260907-Kenna-VT-
Champlain-30_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=2560)North
Beach on Lake Champlain in Burlington in September. Seven of the lake’s 15
sampling stations have exceeded the EPA’s annual phosphorus limits every year
since 2015. Caleb Kenna for ProPublica

One clear opportunity to speed up phosphorus reductions, according to Perkins,
is to ensure farms comply with required agricultural practices and avoid
spreading manure before anticipated rainstorms, which has caused “major
phosphorus runoff events.”

If the state and farm operators were to make that a priority, “it could likely
make a big difference,” Perkins wrote. And the state could encourage that
practice by overhauling its permitting system to tighten water quality
requirements and enforcement for farms that keep animals confined in barns for
long periods of time. Those farms are called concentrated animal feeding
operations, or CAFOs. In recent years, many small family dairies in Vermont
have closed or consolidated into larger operations that would be considered
CAFOs under federal law.

Yet Vermont has delayed action on an EPA directive to strengthen its approach
to regulating CAFOs. Just across the lake, New York has used such permits for
decades to ensure better environmental practices on larger farms. In Vermont,
a recent [state task
force](https://legislature.vermont.gov/Documents/2026/Workgroups/House%20Agriculture/Reports%20and%20Resources/W~Agency%20of%20Natural%20Resources~ACT%2067%20CAFO%20Legislative%20Report%20with%20ANR%20AAFM%20Cover%20Letter~4-30-2026.pdf)
report recommended working to develop this program for another five years.

A second, related reform the EPA has recommended is to change who leads
regulation of those farms.

Vermont has two different agencies that oversee farm pollution. The Agency of
Agriculture regulates how farms handle waste on site, while the Agency of
Natural Resources is responsible if runoff from that waste leaves the farm.
This split responsibility has caused oversight problems, including lapses in
following up on reported water quality violations with inspections and
enforcement actions. Environmental advocates have long maintained that the
agriculture agency has a conflict because it also has a mandate to promote the
state’s farm sector.

![A dead snapping turtle lies on its back on matted
weeds.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20260811_132438_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=527)A
turtle washes up on a high-alert day in St. Albans in August. Lake Champlain
Committee monitor Jon Twombly, courtesy of Lake Champlain Committee

This arrangement frustrates farmers, too. In a letter to Gov. Phil Scott
earlier this year, owners of one Vermont dairy farm wrote that “the lack of
alignment and clear communication between these agencies” places farmers in an
uncertain position. “Many in the farming community feel caught in the middle
of interagency disagreements, unsure which standards will ultimately govern
their operations or how enforcement will proceed,” they wrote.

In interviews, officials at the two agencies acknowledged those communication
problems but said that they have taken steps to improve how they share
information on potential violations and coordinate more closely on
inspections.

In 2024, the EPA ordered Vermont to consolidate the regulation of agricultural
pollution under the Agency of Natural Resources, Vermont’s main environmental
agency, which the EPA says has sole authority to administer federal Clean
Water Act rules.

In a letter that year to Moore, the agency’s secretary, EPA Region 1
administrator David Cash noted that the EPA had monitored the situation in
Vermont for well over a decade. “And despite having had ample time and
opportunity to cure longstanding program deficiencies,” he wrote, “ANR has
failed to do so.” Cash noted that the state has failed to give ANR “sufficient
resources or operational authority” to regulate runoff from farms.

Hovering over this back-and-forth is the threat that the federal government
could take over enforcement of water pollution rules from Vermont.

## [Do You Live Near Lake Champlain? Help Seven Days and ProPublica
Investigate Algae Blooms.](https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/lake-
champlain-vermont-algae-bloom-pollution-callout)

Seven Days and ProPublica have teamed up to investigate the cleanup of Lake
Champlain. Have you been affected by this issue? We’d like to hear from you.

[Get In Touch](https://propublica.jotform.com/263053595887977)

Following the letter to Moore, the divisions between the two agencies were on
display as they discussed their regulatory approach in internal emails
obtained under Vermont’s Public Records Act by Seven Days and ProPublica. In a
2025 email, Agency of Natural Resources general counsel Catherine Gjessing
reminded her counterpart at the agriculture agency and legislative counsel
staff that “there are a significant number of farms that are in fact
discharging without a permit” in violation of the federal Clean Water Act. She
added that the two agencies had been working under this split responsibility
arrangement, with the agriculture agency taking the lead, “for decades now and
we are still not in compliance.”

In an interview, the agriculture agency’s general counsel, Steve Collier, said
there was never “a Wild West situation where farms were not being regulated”
and that his agency’s rules protected the environment. “Whether or not the
Clean Water Act was being administered exactly as it should be is a different
issue,” he said.

Outside of agriculture, Vermont has yet to fully implement a third EPA demand
as well as the directives of its own Clean Water Act. That 2015 law mandated
the Department of Environmental Conservation to require properties with 3 or
more acres of paved surface, such as parking lots, to install systems to slow
and capture stormwater runoff.

Five years later, when the department still hadn’t finalized this “3-acre
rule” permit system, the EPA warned Vermont that it would have to give the
state “a failing grade” if it didn’t do so by Sept. 4, 2020. Vermont met the
EPA’s deadline but in 2025 [passed a
law](https://legislature.vermont.gov/Documents/2026/Docs/ACTS/ACT037/ACT037%20As%20Enacted.pdf)
pushing the date for getting permits to 2028 for properties in the Champlain
basin.

And those property owners don’t need to make the stormwater upgrades until
2033.

### Treading Water

![Green bodies of water frame a narrow road with two small cars pulled off on
the shoulder.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20260819_vtstalbans-67_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg)Algae
blooms in St. Albans in August Caleb Kenna for ProPublica

For a quarter century, Steve Cushing has been advocating to clean up St.
Albans Bay in the northeast part of Lake Champlain near the epicenter of
Vermont’s dairy industry. Throughout that time, he listened as federal and
state environmental officials came through town and pledged to act. "Expect a
lot of progress 10 years from now in many segments of the lake,” one [EPA
official told him and his neighbors in
2015](https://www.mynbc5.com/article/advocates-skeptical-over-new-epa-plan-
for-lake-champlain-cleanup/3324560).

A decade later, this summer’s cyanobacteria blooms in the shallow bay were
some of the worst he’s seen in several years, he said. Since June, the public
beach in the St. Albans Bay Park has mostly been closed to swimming.

“Overall, you can't really see a big improvement in water quality in the bay,”
Cushing said.

Public data supports that notion. Every three years the federally funded Lake
Champlain Basin Program, which coordinates research and grantmaking across the
lake’s watershed, issues a report summarizing its water quality monitoring.

Its most recent edition, from 2024, revealed “deteriorating” trends in the
northeast arm of the lake for both phosphorus and cyanobacteria and no
progress in Missisquoi Bay, a shallow stretch spanning the U.S.-Canada border
that frequently suffers intense blooms.

That’s troubling, scientists and advocates say, because the failure to address
new pollution is exacerbated by both historical pollution and the effects of
climate change.

What scientists call “legacy phosphorus” has accumulated in soils and lake
sediments after many decades of fertilizer use, manure spreading,
deforestation and unregulated septic and wastewater systems.

“We are working on a system that’s been impacted by human activities for the
past 150-plus years,” said Matthew Vaughan, the chief scientist of the basin
program.

Climate change poses another headwind for the lake cleanup. Since 2003,
cyanobacteria blooms have appeared earlier in the spring and later in the fall
as temperatures rise, and even at lower phosphorus levels. The drought that
hit Vermont in 2025 led to a spike in blooms, thanks to the combination of
heat and low water levels. Meanwhile, downpours are turning Vermont’s streams
and rivers into fire hoses of phosphorus-laden sediment: In just one week in
July 2023, record-shattering floods pumped six months worth of phosphorus into
the lake.

“All of this just makes it more urgent to do our part to address these water
quality challenges,” Vaughan said.

Some state officials and researchers contend that phosphorus deposited in the
lake bed and soil decades ago might play as significant a role in fueling
algae blooms as today’s runoff.

![A young woman stands on a boat and holds up white tubing, leaning under the
arch it makes. The boat floats on dark green water, and the sky is
blue.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261019-Kenna-
VT-
Champlain-118_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Caleb
Kenna for ProPublica ![Hands in blue gloves hold a circular filter with
tweezers over a red bucket.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261019-Kenna-VT-
Champlain-228_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Caleb
Kenna for ProPublica

University of Vermont researcher Audrey Manning, first image, collects water
samples on Lake Champlain in Swanton, Vermont, while fellow researcher
Katelynn Warner, second image, gathers cyanobacteria to study their genetic
makeup.

But while legacy phosphorus remains a challenge, “I think it’d be wrong to
just rely on that as the excuse,” said Eric Smeltzer, who worked for the
Department of Environmental Conservation for 35 years, including as the state
limnologist who monitors the health of Vermont’s lakes and ponds.

“The most important technical question about the Lake Champlain phosphorus
cleanup is: Are these practices working? And if not, why not?” Smeltzer said.
“How can it be done better? I think you can’t just explain it away based on
time lags and legacy phosphorus forever.”

In reviewing the state’s data recently, one detail in particular jumped out to
him, he said. Wastewater treatment still garners an outsize share of Vermont’s
clean water spending, even though it has been clear for years that it’s not a
major contributor of phosphorus, while agriculture and stormwater are.

### Read More

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20260819_vtstalbans-38_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1)
**Vermont Was Supposed to Get an Audit of Its Lake Champlain Cleanup. It Never
Happened.** ](https://www.propublica.org/article/vermont-clean-water-act-
champlain-audit)

Cushing traces the algae blooms back to the dairy farms that dominate the
watershed and to regulators’ failure to “put any teeth behind” restrictions on
manure spreading and other water quality rules.

Cushing, a former dairy farmer, has pushed for policy changes as a volunteer
with the St. Albans Area Watershed Association and has led an effort to
mechanically remove vegetation that contributes to the phosphorus problem in
his overburdened bay.

At 78, he is now searching for someone to take over the weed removal effort.
“I’m getting a little burned out,” he admitted.

Seven miles to the west, on the island of North Hero, van den Noort questioned
this summer whether all the data he gathers is making any difference.

“If we really wanted to solve the problem, I think we’d have to make some
tough choices,” he said. “I don’t think anybody wants to do that. It’s a head-
in-the-sand thing.”

Every week, van den Noort drives up the western edge of Isle La Motte on his
monitoring circuit, looking out over a stretch of water that is supposed to be
one of the cleanest parts of Lake Champlain. On the worst days, a pea green
broth of blooms stubbornly hugs its entire shoreline.

with an Adirondack chair, a house and trees can be seen in the
distance.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-

bloom at Lake Champlain at Graveyard Point in North Hero Jeff van den Noort
